The Future Report reveals UK teens use of algorithms, video, and AI for discovery and learning. Navigating trustworthy information is vital and requires a shared effort by platforms, educators, and parents to boost digital literacy, empowering youth to engage in democracy safely.

Rachel Huggins

CEO, Internet Matters

Online spaces are where children and young people discover new ideas, keep up with current events, and learn about the world around them. This is highlighted in Google’s The Future Report, which gathered the views of 6,000 UK teenagers to better understand the opportunities and challenges that technology presents for young people.

For many (83%), information comes through algorithm-driven recommendations — which children see as positive for introducing them to new ideas they may not see otherwise. Young people are also increasingly accessing video-based content and prefer this for building understanding, particularly of difficult topics. They are also engaging with AI, using tools like AI chatbots for creativity and learning on a daily basis.

While the report highlights the positive ways in which the internet is used for discovery and learning, it also points to the challenges young people face in accessing high-quality, trustworthy information. Teens recognised that the proliferation of AI-generated and manipulated content was making the online information environment increasingly complex to navigate. This is echoed in Internet Matters’ own research, which found that the growth of this content is leaving children feeling less trusting of the news they encounter in their feeds and more concerned about their ability to distinguish between what is true and false online.

Addressing these challenges will be essential if we are to preserve the educational benefits of online spaces. Children and young people must have access to high-quality, accurate content, alongside the skills to critically engage in an increasingly complex information environment. This is especially important in the UK, which is set to lower the voting age to 16, with the aim of increasing lifelong democratic participation. However, this will only be possible if young people feel equipped to engage confidently with the news, politics and current affairs they encounter online.

Encouragingly, Google’s research found that many teenagers are already using strategies to verify online information, including cross-checking sources (49%), checking the credibility of websites and authors (48%) and speaking to parents and trusted adults about the content they have seen online (45%). However, the responsibility for navigating a changing and complex information environment should not rest with young people alone.

Platforms, educators, and policymakers all have a role to play in helping children and young people access trustworthy information and develop digital and media literacy. Schools must be supported with clear direction set by government, alongside the resources and training needed to teach these skills effectively in the classroom. Tech companies also have an important role to play by making their platforms and services safe and media-literate by design. This means supporting children to have age-appropriate experiences and embedding features that help young people evaluate, question and contextualise what they see.

Parents will also continue to be children’s main source of information about online safety, and who they turn to when they need support. Yet they are also navigating many of the same challenges as their children. As a result, we must ensure that they too feel confident and able to support children — whether this is through building their own media literacy skills, improving access to easy-to-use parental controls or providing advice on where to access high-quality content.

Through this shared approach, we can build a safer and more empowering digital environment where every young person can confidently participate and thrive.

Supporting the findings of the 2026 Future research, Childnet’s new research reveals how teenagers are embracing AI creatively and responsibly, emphasising the vital role of listening to young voices and supporting families in navigating online safety.

Will Gardner

CEO, Childnet

Childnet has worked towards making the internet a great and safe place for over 30 years; however, it feels like concerns around online safety have never been higher. Whilst these conversations around online safety are happening, it is crucial that children and young people’s perspectives are taken into account.

At Childnet, youth voice is at the heart of everything we do, and we pride ourselves on not just listening to young people, but having their opinions shape everything we do. Young people tell us they believe that change is needed online and that significantly more needs to be done to make the online world a safe and positive space.

## Why we need to listen to young people

Google’s The Future Report, which spoke to more than 6,000 UK teenagers, found that 67% use AI tools creatively daily. This mass adoption of this technology is very much in line with our own research released in February for Safer Internet Day 2026 , which found that nearly all young people aged 8 to 17 (97%) use AI tools, with 58% saying that AI makes their lives better.

Our research found that young people liked to use AI for a variety of reasons, with 71% of young people saying that AI saves them a lot of time, while a growing number are using it for help and support, with 64% agreeing that AI is the best way to get advice quickly.

Both pieces of work show that young people are aware of the risks or challenges which come with spending time online, and of the impact of an overreliance on AI and other emerging technologies.

We found that 41% of teens feel like people their age are relying heavily on AI for emotional support or help with emotional issues, while almost one in seven (14%) say they use AI tools to discuss things they don’t feel they can talk to anyone else about. This could also be seen across The Future report, where almost a fifth (18%) of teens surveyed (and 20% of 16-18s) reported chatting to AI "as a friend".

We also can’t ignore the real fears that young people have shared about AI, with 60% of young people saying they are concerned about someone using AI to make inappropriate pictures of them, as well as concerns around the impact on creativity and schoolwork, and even for emotional support or friendship.

Through our work in schools, our youth advisory boards, and in our focus groups, we see time and time again that young people are not only willing to have conversations about their life online, but that they are eager to have their voices heard about the issues that matter most to them.

## The role of parents and carers

Parents and carers play a key role in supporting their children online. Our research found that 74% of young people would talk to a parent or carer if they were worried about AI; however parents and carers need more support and resources too. Less than 1 in 5 parents have set rules or guidelines for how their child can use AI at home and only 13% know where to go for advice or support if they are worried about their child’s use of AI.

The Future report also showed young people who were willing to have these conversations with their parents and carers. Approximately three in ten teens indicated that allowing their parents to supervise their online activities (30%) was a helpful measure.

At Childnet, we have a range of free resources to help parents, carers, and educators have conversations with young people about their life online, including our Family Agreement, conversation starters , and youth voice in online safety toolkit . We also have specific resources designed to talk about AI , both in the classroom and at home.

There is a feeling of a state of flux, of often rapid change, in both technology and the rules around access to technology – in this context, education and conversations which take on board young people’s experience will be more important than ever.

The Future Report reveals UK teens are curious, digitally confident, and critical of online content. Rather than viewing technology solely through fear, policies should support youth and parents together—fostering resilience, media literacy, and safe, empowering AI use.

Vicki Shotbolt

CEO, ParentZone

Read the Future Report and you meet a generation that is curious, capable and far more thoughtful about technology than we often give them credit for. Of the 6,000 UK teenagers surveyed, 77% said they always or often stop to consider whether what they find online can be trusted. That should make us optimistic, and it should inform how we think about keeping them safe.

Too often, public debates frame young people's digital lives as problems to be solved. Screen time to cut, platforms to restrict, harms to count. The report describes teenagers who are "digitally confident, curious and optimistic" while staying alert to the risks. That is much closer to what we hear from parents, who know what a great generation they are raising. They have concerns, but they also see children who are creative, funny and often remarkably sensible online. If policy starts only from fear, we risk designing for the worst case and failing everyone else.

When we think about online safety, we usually list what we hope to prevent. The risks are real, and parents are right to want them gone. But there is a second list we rarely write down and that one includes what gets lost when we take access away. The learning, the creativity, the conversations and the confidence that come from using technology well.

Those skills need to be developed over time in age appropriate ways. Knowing to check what you're consuming online is something that is learned through practice and with support. Trying things, getting some wrong, and working out what to do differently builds resilience. You can see it grow with age. The report tells us that 52% of 16 to 18 year olds always check what they find, compared with 33% of 13 to 15 year olds.

That learning takes place with the help, guidance, and involvement of parents and teachers Eighty-one percent of teens say they would ask a parent for help with misinformation, scams or cyberbullying, and that barely drops as they get older (83% of 13 to 15s, 79% of 16 to 18s). Teens want their parents involved with three in ten saying that parental supervision helps them get the balance right.

The same goes for AI. Two thirds of teens use it at least a couple of times a week, for creative projects (67%) or learning (65%). What's striking is how they use it. They value AI when it helps them understand, not just when it gives answers. One 15-year-old in the report said she needs to know "how it's been worked out" for her schoolwork. That is exactly the instinct parents and educators want to develop.

If we can, the opportunities are incredible. Older teens are already using AI to learn a language (20%), teach themselves to code (19%) and prepare for job applications (17%). This is a generation using technology to stretch themselves, and as an organisation dedicated to improving outcomes for children that’s exciting to read.

There is clearly more work to be done. The report is honest about the gap teenagers perceive. Twenty-six percent of older teens worry their parents can't recognise AI or fake content. Parents need to be brought on the journey to an AI enabled world alongside everyone else. They need platforms that are safe by design, the confidence to respond calmly when things go wrong, and the chance to learn about AI alongside their children.

This generation is giving us real reasons to be hopeful. Our job is to make sure every child gets to build these skills, with the adults in their lives beside them.

This July, as the Railroad Fire spread through Washington overnight, Watch Duty sent its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert to its users. It started with a 911 dispatch buried in radio static — and a new Gemini tool that caught it in seconds.

A dedicated team of Google engineers and researchers spent six months embedded full-time with Watch Duty , a nonprofit wildfire alert app run by active and retired firefighters, dispatchers, and first responders. Through the Google.org Fellowship, they used more than 20,000 hours of past radio recordings to build a Gemini-powered tool that wipes out heavy static and translates specialized firefighting terminology into clean, searchable text. The system removes the added strain of deciphering noisy audio so volunteers can focus on verifying incidents and getting alerts out.

## The challenge

When a wildfire starts, minutes can decide whether people get out safely. Yet across much of the country, the first word of a new fire still travels over decades-old analog VHF radio, where engine noise, wind, static, and rapid-fire tactical jargon make it hard to hear what's happening. Watch Duty reporters monitor up to 20 feeds manually, making it a challenge to cut through the noise.

## The results

Across Watch Duty's network, the tool has:

- Helped close coverage gaps in areas with no other automated dispatch detection, sending reporters a signal in less than 30 seconds; this way, a new fire isn't missed just because no one was listening at that moment

- Reduced word error rate on degraded VHF radio audio from 38% down to 22.34%

- Transcribed more than 200 hours of radio speech a day from about 400 active feeds, and has been designed and tested to handle more than 10,000 feeds at once.

As a result of the collaboration between Google and Watch Duty, volunteer reporter satisfaction with radio transcription tools increased from 35.3% to 92.3%.

The tool was also put to test during a live fire. In July 2026, a fast-moving wildfire — the Railroad Fire — ignited at night in Washington. When the first 911 dispatch went out over local fire radio, the Gemini-powered transcription tool transcribed it straight from the noisy radio audio and flagged it in under 30 seconds.

That head start gave Watch Duty's team the time they needed to verify the fire and push a Critical Alert—which breaks through do-not-disturb mode in urgent situations—helping residents evacuate before flames reached homes. It was the first time Watch Duty had ever sent a Critical Alert overnight, proving what faster detection means when communities are asleep and every minute counts.

## The collaboration

The new AI radio tool is the latest milestone in a deep, multi-year collaboration spanning Google's philanthropic, product, and research teams to help Watch Duty scale its life-saving mission across all 50 states.

- Funding : In 2024, Google.org provided Watch Duty with $2 million in funding and $300,000 in Google Cloud credits to help compile satellite, camera, and radio data to validate new fires.

- Search : During US fires such as the Palisades, Eaton, Hurst, and Auto fires, Google Search featured Watch Duty in SOS alerts alongside official emergency guidance.

- Alerts at scale : Watch Duty sends push alerts through Firebase Cloud Messaging. As its audience grew to more than 16 million people last year, Google Cloud raised its messaging limit from 600,000 to 1 million to help alerts arrive without delay.

- Broader industry partnership : As part of the AI Collaborative: Wildfires , Watch Duty is turning models and data into tools that agencies, communities, and responders trust and use.

When the next fire starts, the goal is simple: get people the warning they need while there's still time to act.

## Introducing MKA

Most knowledge work benchmarks can be solved with text alone, without ever needing to look at an image or page layout. Yet, everyday professional work looks very different. Across many industries, day-to-day work is deeply visual — from cross-referencing architectural blueprints and tracing engineering schematics to synthesizing findings into polished decks, reports, and spreadsheets. Your genome is your body’s instruction manual: the blueprint that informs how your body functions. It contains 3 billion base pairs of DNA. Because this DNA is responsible in part for switching genes on and off, it could be the difference between developing a disease and avoiding one. Determining which DNA changes cause diseases (and other outcomes) is like finding a needle in a haystack.

Illustrative. Your genome, one point at a time.

Decoding the DNA sequence is the goal behind AlphaGenome , a model from Google DeepMind. AlphaGenome can take a partial DNA sequence of 1 million base pairs in length, and make thousands of predictions. By comparing these predictions for DNA changes, scientists can find that needle faster.

We talked to Google DeepMind research scientist Žiga Avsec to learn more.

What do you do at Google?

ŽA: I’m a research scientist overseeing our genomics initiative. Basically, I lead a team that builds models to help us better understand the genome.

How is your team making it easier for scientists to predict and understand diseases?

It really all comes down to how the genome works. It contains 3 billion DNA base pairs. And each pair contains two bases, which we call “letters.” These letters — A (adenine), T (thymine), C (cytosine), G (guanine) — act like a biological alphabet, spelling out the genetic instruction manual that makes someone who they are.

Since you can replace any of those letters with three other letters, there are 9 billion possible single-letter changes. Many genetic diseases are caused by just one of these letters changing. But scientists don’t have time to run billions of studies to figure out which changes make a difference.

So we used AlphaGenome to predict the outcomes of all 9 billion single-letter changes, and we created a massive dataset — AlphaGenome Atlas — so scientists can decide what to research faster.

Illustrative. The letters are invented for this example.

What’s holding scientists back from better understanding the genome?

While science can read all 3 billion base pairs of human DNA, we still haven’t fully deciphered the semantics of the genetic code — particularly the non-coding "dark matter" that regulates gene expression and disease risk. Experimental research, or as it’s also called, wet-lab research is the best way to help us reach breakthroughs in our understanding, but it’s expensive and time-consuming. A single breakthrough could take years.

Let’s say you sequence DNA from a patient with a rare disease. You might end up with 4 million variants — 4 million ways their DNA differs from the standard reference human genome. But the question is: Which variant is causing their condition? Maybe you narrow the list to only include rare variants. But even then, you could be left with hundreds or thousands of options.

When scientists use AlphaGenome Atlas, they get a single, easy-to-read score — the AVI (AlphaGenome Variant Impact) score — which instantly indicates the potential impact of a variant across the full genome. This helps them prioritize and more easily find the most disruptive changes to follow up on.

Illustrative. Each dot stands for many variants. Scores are invented.

Can you give me some examples of how AlphaGenome impacts everyday people?

Tools like AlphaGenome move us from merely reading DNA to helping us better understand the molecular mechanisms behind a disease, giving researchers new leads to test and taking an important step towards someday digitally simulating a complete human cell.

There are several ways that will have an impact. It can accelerate research that could help society improve our ability to diagnose and personalize treatment for patients suffering from rare or previously uncharacterized genetic disorders. It could also speed up drug discovery pipelines by helping pharmaceutical researchers identify and validate high-probability therapeutic targets faster. Beyond healthcare, AlphaGenome’s model architecture could help researchers tackle broader societal challenges, including breeding climate-resilient crops.

Illustrative. Possible ways AlphaGenome can help.

What kinds of breakthroughs has AlphaGenome enabled?

AlphaGenome is still pretty new. We launched it in June 2025, and we just introduced AlphaGenome Atlas in September this year. But researchers are already using it to advance science.

Gareth Hawkes, a Medical Research Council fellow at the University of Exeter, used AlphaGenome Atlas to narrow down a list of 1 billion genetic variants. By focusing on the most impactful 1%, he identified 19 variant groups linked to body mass index to prioritize in his research.

And Laura Covill, a Broad Institute research fellow, used the AVI score to prioritize genetic variants in their research of unsolved rare diseases. AlphaGenome Atlas identified a critical variant in a gene linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, providing crucial supporting evidence that drove their subsequent research, including solving the case.

What are you hoping to do next?

We just launched our latest model, AlphaGenome 2 , which tackles one of the key limitations of AlphaGenome: cell type specificity. While AlphaGenome is state-of-the-art, it was trained mostly on data from whole tissues or cell lines. We know that individual cell types in those tissues have a very specific role and can malfunction in disease. AlphaGenome 2 moves beyond tissue-level averages to predict how genetic variants disrupt these individual cell types, helping researchers pinpoint the cellular drivers of disease.

We’re also actively researching better ways to measure how confident our model is in its predictions so researchers know how much to trust each result. From early analyses, we see that variants with strongly predicted effects are quite good and achieve high levels of accuracy. As always, anyone using AlphaGenome should interpret its predictions with other sources of information.

What's the ultimate goal of your work in biology?

In the short term, we’d like to use AI to better understand the grammar of the genome and accurately predict the effects of mutations. In the long term, we’d like to build on this foundation towards a fully functioning digital simulation of a human cell.

This will allow researchers to computationally model disease mechanisms, understand rare genetic conditions, and test candidate therapies.

When an agent connects to dozens or even hundreds of tools, sending every full parameter schema on every request adds up fast. It inflates input token counts, adds latency, and lowers tool-selection accuracy as the candidate list grows. Tool Retrieval lets your agent keep its full tool library on standby and load parameter schemas only when the current task needs them.

## How it works

To turn on Tool Retrieval, add a tool_search tool to your request and set defer_loading: true on the tools you want to hold back. The model still sees the name and description of every deferred tool, so it knows what's available, but the parameter schemas stay out of context. When the model needs a tool, it asks for it by name, the API loads the full schema, and the model calls the function, all inside the same request.

from google import genai client = genai.Client() tools = [ {"type": "tool_search"}, { "type": "function", "name": "issue_refund", "description": "Refund an order to the original payment method.", "defer_loading": True, "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "order_id": {"type": "string"}, "amount": {"type": "number"}, }, "required": ["order_id", "amount"], }, }, # ... 50+ other deferred functions (leave frequent tools undeferred) ] interaction = client.interactions.create( model="gemini-4-hydrogen", input="Order A-1042 arrived damaged. Please refund 40 dollars.", tools=tools, )

Inside that single API call, the model searches for issue_refund , the API loads its schema, and the model emits the function_call . All three steps appear in interaction.steps , making it easy to inspect which tools the model considered when debugging tool names or descriptions:

"steps": [ { "type": "tool_search_call", "id": "tsc_7f2a", "arguments": {"function_names": ["issue_refund"]}, "signature": "..." }, { "type": "tool_search_result", "call_id": "tsc_7f2a", "result": [{"type": "function", "name": "issue_refund", "parameters": {...}}], "signature": "..." }, { "type": "function_call", "id": "fc_91c3", "name": "issue_refund", "arguments": {"order_id": "A-1042", "amount": 40} } ]

From here it's normal function calling: your code runs the refund and sends back a function_result .

There's no index to build or host. Gemini runs the search on the server, so the only changes to your code are the new tool and a flag on the tools you want to defer. You can keep your most-used tools loaded up front and defer the long tail.

Tool Retrieval also plays well with prefix caching. Deferred schemas stay out of the start of the prompt, and the schemas the model loads are added later in the conversation, so the cached prefix stays the same from turn to turn.

Tool Retrieval also works with remote MCP servers in the Gemini API . Set defer_loading: true on an mcp_server tool and every tool that server exposes is loaded on demand, so you can connect a large server without listing its tools one by one.

## How client-side retrieval works

If you maintain your own tool registry, embedding index, or per-user permission filter, declare the tool_search with "execution": "client" and define your search parameters. Client-side retrieval adds one round trip per search, because your app runs the lookup. Tools do not need to be declared upfront, so you can also expose new tools mid-conversation when a user connects an integration:

tools = [{ "type": "tool_search", "execution": "client", "name": "search_tools", "description": "Search the internal tool registry for functions.", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["query"], }, }] # When the model emits a function_call for "search_tools", # return matching {"type": "function", ...} schemas in function_result: followup = client.interactions.create( model="gemini-4-hydrogen", previous_interaction_id=interaction.id, tools=tools, input=[{ "type": "function_result", "name": "search_tools", "call_id": step.id, "result": my_registry.search(**step.arguments), }], )

## How pricing and supported models work

Tool Retrieval has no separate charge. Input and output tokens are billed at the standard rates for the model you call. Turning on tool_search adds a small, fixed block of input tokens, and each schema the model loads is billed as input for the rest of the conversation, the same as a tool declared up front. You save tokens when the schemas you never load outweigh the ones you do, which is the usual case for large libraries. Measure it against your own traffic.

The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. ## Strong performance and calibration

On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error.

Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.

## Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass

Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.

You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer:

- noul (Yes/No): Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.

- choice (Multiple Choice): Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate.

- score (Ordered Rubric): Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.

Technology best serves education when it creates space for inspiring teaching and deeper learning. To better understand how AI tools perform in everyday educational settings, we’ve spent the past year working alongside educators and researchers in classrooms across the UK and Italy.

From testing one-on-one AI math tutoring to analyzing thousands of hours of classroom collaboration, today we’re sharing new research findings that demonstrate the impact of this technology on the process of teaching and learning. Together, the results show that AI tutoring using Gemini capabilities can deliver support on par with human tutors for UK students when used responsibly with human oversight, while Gemini itself can foster more collaborative classrooms and support teacher wellbeing in Italy.

## UK: Scaling reliable, effective math tutoring

To truly understand how student learning is being shaped, we need to study it over time across diverse classroom settings. We previously ran an exploratory study with Eedi , which found that AI tutoring could operate effectively in real classrooms. The study tested an AI tutor combining Gemini capabilities with Eedi's study platform, designed to identify a student’s specific mistake and guide them to fix it themselves.

This year, we set out to better understand Gemini's pedagogical capabilities and the nuances of student learning in structured mathematics lessons. We conducted a 10-week randomized controlled trial (RCT) with over 1,100 students (ages 12-15) in the UK to measure their learning gains in math through sessions on Eedi’s school platform. Educators were actively involved at every stage of the study — with teachers monitoring student progress and providing hands-on support in the classroom, and tutors guiding students one-on-one through the platform.

Whenever a student answered a question incorrectly, they received one of three types of support: a static hint, help from a human tutor, or interactive AI tutoring combining Eedi’s pedagogical resources with Gemini. To ensure teaching quality, human experts reviewed every AI response in real time before it reached a student. While test scores aren’t the only measure of learning outcomes, over the course of the trial, we tracked their progress across regular assignments in the Eedi platform, intermediate quizzes, and independent STAR standardized tests.

This trial revealed major leaps in model quality and student performance. Compared to last year’s study, Gemini’s pedagogical quality improved by nearly 25%, increasing the outright approval rate by expert reviewers from 76% to 95%. Across in-platform tasks and intermediate quizzes, students receiving AI tutoring performed similarly to those paired with human tutors. Just as importantly, AI tutoring promoted active thinking rather than shortcuts: following a pedagogical prompt we provided, Gemini guided students instead of handing them answers in nearly 99% of sessions, and students worked through the math themselves in more than 85% of their chats.

While the use of AI tutoring led to clear gains on daily classroom tasks and quizzes, these gains didn’t show up on STAR standardized test scores over the same trial period. After exploring more, we believe this can be attributed to step-by-step tutoring taking more time per question than using simple hints. Students in the trial therefore solved fewer total problems per session (averaging about 14 with AI tutoring versus 19 with static hints). Over 10 weeks, that lower volume meant students covered less overall curriculum material—even as their pacing and understanding improved—indicating the trial length wasn't long enough to cover the broad range of topics on the STAR test. To examine this trend further, we are exploring follow-up trials across a full academic year while also expanding our metrics to better understand what drives meaningful learning and eventual outcomes.

You can find more details in our full technical report .

## Italy: Creating a more active classroom

Following our initial pilot in Northern Italy , we worked with the Salesians of Don Bosco school network and the Pontifical Salesian University in Rome on a yearlong study across 31 schools. Together, we learned from Primary, Secondary and Vocational educators across 1,600 teachers (representing over 24,500 students ages 13-18) by collecting classroom activities and self reports on lesson planning both with and without Gemini for Education to understand how AI supports classroom dynamics, student engagement, and teacher wellbeing.

The findings show that AI is most effective when educators remain at the center of the classroom and learning. When educators used Gemini to co-design lessons, they reported feeling more creative than usual in their teaching and planning (79% with Gemini vs. 30% without Gemini) — a shift that helped transform classroom dynamics. Traditional front of the classroom lectures dropped by 38%, making way for workshops, group activities and peer discussions that nearly tripled student-led collaborative learning. In turn, students responded positively to the collaborative environment and active lessons created by their teachers. In lessons teachers co-designed with Gemini, more students actively participated in class (with student reported engagement rising from 77% to 84%) while debating diverse viewpoints more often and taking greater ownership of their learning.

Beyond improving classroom dynamics, the study showed a meaningful impact on teacher wellbeing. Educators often carry the heavy burden of relying solely on their own energy to keep a room engaged but in lessons co-planned with Gemini, that reliance dropped by 66%. Instead, lessons where the activity design itself drove engagement more than doubled (from 23.2% to 52.2%), carrying the momentum of the class and relieving some of that daily pressure of keeping students engaged.

Even on days with tight prep time, having AI as a thought partner to adapt materials gave educators the support they needed to focus on what matters most: mentoring and connecting with their students. More details about the implementation and study can be found in the Don Bosco CNOS-FAP Foundation implementation report .
